replays.prompt: Did my last change make the persons service slower? Jeffrey has "persons direct" from before the change and "persons dom" from after it.

runs.reply:
**Probably yes.** The "persons dom" run does measurably more work than "persons direct", mostly in the database. This is one pair of recordings, so treat it as strong evidence, not proof.

**Comparability.** [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) is the primary (after) and [persons direct ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a) is the baseline (before). The two were recorded the same way: 76.09 s against 76.09 s, and 107 shared event types have matching settings. The wall-clock sampler's settings are unknown for both runs. Whether both runs did the same work isn't shown by the recordings. The HTTP exchange counts are nearly equal (12,348 against 12,349), which suggests the same request volume. Neither profile carries a commit, so I haven't tied any of this to your diff. Here is the [differential in Microscope ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraphs/differential?baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a).

| Measure (about the same requests) | direct | dom | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU samples (`jdk.ExecutionSample`) | 4,628 | 5,097 | +10% |
| Bytes allocated | 3.24 GB | 4.10 GB | +26% |
| JDBC queries | 11,148 | 15,122 | +36% |
| Connections acquired | 12,339 | 16,318 | +32% |
| Monitor-blocked time | 179 ms | 672 ms | about 3.8× |

**CPU.** The [CPU differential ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ExecutionSample&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782) shows the growth in SQLite native code:
- `libc.so.6` (`__libc_pread` under `NativeDB#step`) grew by 271 samples (+42.5%, +4.05 pp of the profile).
- The `libsqlitejdbc` library grew by 74 samples (+89%).
- The baseline's second `libsqlitejdbc` row, which drops to 0, is the same library extracted to a differently named temp file. It isn't a real improvement.
- Most of the other movers are JIT compiler frames (`Phase*`, `Node::*`) and JFR internals. Those are profiler and warm-up noise, not your code.

**Allocation.** The [allocation differential ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&useWeight=true&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782) is dominated by `byte[]` (+379 MiB) and by `jdk.jfr.consumer` and `PrettyWriter` frames. Those frames are the JFR tooling reading its own recording, so they inflate the total and I wouldn't blame them on your change.

**Candidate rename.** The comparison flags `EfficientPersonService#getNPersons` and `#getRandomPerson` as vanished, and the `InefficientPersonService` versions as appeared. They allocate almost the same amount (184 MiB against 178.5 MiB, and 61 MiB against 54.5 MiB). Only the service class differs, so this is a swap and not an allocation regression.

**Interpretation.** With the same number of requests, about 36% more queries and 32% more connection acquisitions point to more database round-trips per request. That fits the extra time in SQLite's `pread` and the extra lock contention. This is a hypothesis from the counts. I haven't read your diff to confirm it.

**Limits.**
- This is CPU samples, allocation and counts. It doesn't measure end-to-end latency.
- A +10% CPU move from one pair of runs can't be separated from run-to-run variance. The query-count and connection-count jumps are much larger and less likely to be noise.
- I looked at CPU samples and allocation only. I didn't read the monitor-contention call paths, so I haven't located the cause of the 3.8× rise.

If you tell me which commit is "the last change", I can map these movements onto its diff. Otherwise I can follow the extra queries to the call sites that issue them.

**Yes, on CPU and allocation the "persons dom" profile is heavier than "persons direct". It looks like extra database work per request.** I can't say whether end-to-end latency got worse, because these profiles don't measure it.

**Comparability.** The two recordings were made the same way: 76.09 s against 76.09 s, and all 107 shared event types with stored settings match. The one exception is `profiler.WallClockSample`, whose settings are unknown on both sides. Whether the two runs did the same work isn't shown. Both HTTP server event counts are almost identical (12,348 against 12,349), which suggests similar request volume. Jeffrey can't confirm that, so I can't make any per-request claim from the counts alone. Neither profile records a commit, so pairing them with your last change is your word, not something the data shows. Both start within 2 ms of each other, which is odd if they were separate runs. Comparison: [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) (primary, after) against [persons direct ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a) (baseline, before).

**What moved**

| Measure | direct (before) | dom (after) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU samples (`jdk.ExecutionSample`) | 4,628 | 5,097 | +10% |
| Allocation (`jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`) | 3.0 GiB | 3.8 GiB | +26% |

- **CPU:** [the differential flamegraph ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ExecutionSample&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782) shows most of the growth in native SQLite code. `libc.so.6` (reached through `pread`) gained 271 samples (+42%) and the SQLite library gained 74 (+89%). `String#indexOf` gained 37 (+51%). The rest are small movements in JIT compiler frames, which I'd treat as noise.
- **Allocation:** the biggest movers are `byte[]` (+379 MiB), `ArrayList$Itr` (+189 MiB) and `String` (+87 MiB). Several of the top allocation paths run through `jdk.jfr` consumer and printing code, which looks like profiler or tooling overhead, not application code. `int[]` is up 14 MiB, with its example path through `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion` and `String#replaceAll`, which compiles a regex on each call.
- **Candidate renames:** [the allocation comparison ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&useWeight=true&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782) pairs `InefficientPersonService#getNPersons` and `#getRandomPerson` (after) with `EfficientPersonService` (before). They allocate about the same (184 MiB against 178.5 MiB, and 61 MiB against 54.5 MiB). So this is a switch of implementation class, not a new cost inside either method.

**Confidence: medium.** This is one pair of runs with no repetition, so the CPU movement (+10%) could partly be run-to-run variance. The query and connection counts (+32–36% at equal HTTP volume) are the stronger signal. The monitor-blocking figure comes from a type the differential tools don't rank, so it hasn't been checked per method.

I haven't tied this to your diff. There are no Java sources in this working directory, so I couldn't read your change or check `PersonRepository`.

- Read the JDBC statements with `jdbc_statementGroup` to see which queries multiplied.
- Look at monitor contention with `blocking_monitors` on the dom profile.

**Comparability.** The two runs were recorded the same way: 76.09 s against 76.09 s, 107 shared event types with matching settings, and the same HTTP request count (12,348 against 12,349). **What moved** (figures are for the whole recording, after against before):

| Measure | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU samples (`jdk.ExecutionSample`) | 4,628 | 5,097 | +10% |
| JDBC queries | 11,148 | 15,122 | +36% |

The CPU growth is mostly in native SQLite: `libc.so.6` (`pread`) rose by 271 samples (+42.5%, +4.05 pp of the profile) and the SQLite JDBC library by 74 samples (+89%). The old and new SQLite library paths show up as different files because the temp file name changes per run. That is not a code change.
- **Allocation is up 26.5%.** The biggest rises are in `byte[]` (+379 MiB) and `ArrayList$Itr`, `String` and `char[]`. `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion` allocates through `String#replaceAll`, which recompiles a regex `Pattern` on every call. replays.prompt: We rolled out a new build of the persons service. In Jeffrey, "persons direct" is the build before and "persons dom" is the new one. Did the new build make the service slower, and where?

runs.reply:
**Yes, the new build is slower, but only modestly: about 10% more CPU samples, 27% more allocation, and 36% more database queries for the same number of requests. The extra cost is in database access and string/regex work.** I can't tell you this is a measured end-to-end latency regression.

**How far the comparison can be trusted.** [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) is the primary (new build). [persons direct ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a) is the baseline (old build).
- The two were recorded the same way. They ran 76.09 s against 76.09 s, both used async-profiler, and 107 shared event types have matching settings. The only exception is the wall-clock sampler, whose settings were not stored for either side.
- The workload looks the same size: 12,348 HTTP exchanges against 12,349. That is an observed count only, so equal work is not proven.
- Neither profile has a recorded commit, so I can't tie any movement to a diff.
- This is a single pair of runs, so small movements could be run-to-run noise.

**What moved** ([differential view ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraphs/differential?baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a)):

1. **Database work.** The new build runs more queries for the same traffic.
   - JDBC queries went from 11,148 to 15,122 (+36%), and connection acquisitions from 12,339 to 16,318 (+32%).
   - CPU samples (`jdk.ExecutionSample`, 5,097 against 4,628, +10%) shifted into the SQLite native layer. Time in `libc` under `NativeDB#step` (mostly `__libc_pread`) rose from 638 to 909 samples (+4.05 pp of the profile). The SQLite library itself rose from 83 to 157 (+89%).
   - A low-level read inside SQLite's step call fits more queries hitting disk. Querying the same data more often (an N+1 pattern) would explain it, but this profile doesn't show that.

2. **Allocation.** Allocation weight (`jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`) rose from 3.0 GiB to 3.8 GiB (+27%), and GC events went from 20 to 24.
   - `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion` calls `String#replaceAll`, which compiles a regex on every call. Its `int[]` allocation rose +14 MiB (+42%).
   - String splitting rose +87 MiB (+32%).
   - The biggest raw increases, `byte[]` (+379 MiB, +25%) and `ArrayList$Itr` (+189 MiB, +38%), are mostly the profiling and JFR-reading machinery, not application code.
   - `InefficientPersonService#getNPersons` and `getRandomPerson` appear only in the new build, and `EfficientPersonService` equivalents only in the old one. Their sizes match closely (184 MiB against 178.5 MiB for `getNPersons`). This looks like the service implementation was swapped. That is a suggestion from names and sizes, not something I confirmed in source.

3. **Lock contention.** `jdk.JavaMonitorEnter` blocked time went from 179 ms to 672 ms (3.8×), with 586 events against 556. I did not rank which monitors, so this is only a lead.

4. **Wall clock and JIT.** Nothing meaningful moved on wall-clock time. The other CPU increases are JIT compiler (C2) noise, which fits the 409 against 369 deoptimizations and is not an application change.

**Not shown.** This doesn't measure request latency. Wall-clock samples barely moved, so the extra CPU, allocation and queries may not add much latency.

The classes named above (`InefficientPersonService`, `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion`) are not in this working directory, so I can't map the movements to source or offer code changes here.

**Next steps, if you want them:** rank the contended monitors with `blocking_monitors`; find which statements account for the extra queries with `jdbc_overview`; or point me at the persons service repository and the two commits so I can tie these to the diff.

**Short answer:** the new build did more work for the same number of requests, mostly database work. CPU time rose about 10% and allocation about 27%. I haven't measured request latency, so I can't say the service got slower end to end.

**What can be compared.** [persons dom ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0) is the primary and [persons direct ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a) is the baseline.
- The two were recorded the same way. Both are async-profiler recordings of 76.09 s and 76.09 s, 107 shared types have matching settings, and no findings were raised. The wall-clock sampler's settings couldn't be read on either side.
- Whether both runs did the same work is not shown. The best hint is that they served the same number of HTTP exchanges (12,348 against 12,349), but that count isn't proof of equal workload.
- Neither profile has a `recordingCommit`, so I can't tie the movements to a diff.
- Every figure below comes from a single pair of runs, so small moves could be noise.

**Where it got slower** (differential: [CPU ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ExecutionSample&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782), [allocation ↗](http://localhost:8585/profiles/01a1afdf-87cc-76e1-8817-519cae161ef0/flamegraph-view?eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB&graphMode=DIFFERENTIAL&baseline=01a1afdf-762e-70e6-8b67-261e858ea04a&useWeight=true&startEpochMs=1793733180689&endEpochMs=1793733256782))

1. **More SQL per request, in SQLite.**
   - The new build ran 15,122 JDBC queries against 11,148 (+36%) and borrowed 16,318 connections against 12,339 (+32%), for the same request count.
   - CPU samples rose from 4,628 to 5,097 (+10%). Most of the increase is native SQLite work: `libc.so.6` (`__libc_pread` under `NativeDB#step`) went from 638 to 909 samples (+271, +4.05 pp of the profile).
   - The SQLite native library went from 83 to 157 samples. The baseline also shows 22 samples in a differently named copy of the same library (`sqlite-…-40f3afff…`). Treating the two copies as one library, it went from 105 to 157 (+50%).
   - So the extra queries are reading more data from disk.
2. **More allocation.** TLAB allocation rose from 3.0 GiB to 3.8 GiB per run (+26.5%) and young GCs from 18 to 22.
   - The growth is mostly `byte[]` (+379 MiB), `ArrayList$Itr`, `String` and `StringBuilder`.
   - One code path in the allocation ranking, `PersonRepository#modifyOpinion`, compiles a regex with `String#replaceAll` on each call. Its `int[]` and `Pattern` allocation moved by only a few MiB, so I'm not blaming it.
   - Much of the rest of the allocation ranking is the JFR consumer and printer classes (`jdk.jfr.consumer`, `PrettyWriter`), not the application's own code.
3. **Candidate renames.** The allocation ranking pairs `EfficientPersonService#getNPersons` and `#getRandomPerson` in the baseline with `InefficientPersonService` versions in the new build. Their sizes are nearly equal (184 MiB against 178.5 MiB, and 61 MiB against 54.5 MiB), so they don't explain the +0.8 GiB. I haven't read the source, so I can't tell a rename from a real change.

**What did not move.** Wall-clock (idle excluded) shows no meaningful movement. The top frame is the same idle `libc.so.6` wait, +10 samples out of about 35,900 on each side. The remaining CPU movers are small: `String#indexOf` (+37) and C2 compiler frames, which are JIT noise.

**Leads I haven't checked:**
- Blocked time on monitors was 672 ms against 179 ms (3.8×), with 586 against 556 events. The differential tools don't compare that event type, so it needs a single-profile look at `jdk.JavaMonitorEnter` in each run.

- `NPlusOnePersonService.getNPersons` (`NPlusOnePersonService.java:40-50`) picks `count` ids. It then maps each one through `repository::findById` inside a `person.load-each` span.
- Each `findById` runs its own `find_by_id` statement (`PersonRepository.java:111`, via `DatabaseClient.querySingle`).
- That makes 1 id-picking step plus `count` queries per request. The class's own javadoc says the efficient service runs a single `find_all_by_ids` instead.

- The ~25 per request is my arithmetic from those counts. I didn't pull a single `GET /persons/{count}` trace to confirm the statements run one after another.

**Fix**
Replace the stream with one batched query by id list, as `EfficientPersonService` already does. I haven't changed anything. I can apply that change if you want, or check the result with a re-profile.

Record it with JFR. It needs nothing installed, and Jeffrey reads it directly.

**1. Start the service with a recording flag**

```
-XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,filename=/absolute/path/persons.jfr,dumponexit=true -Dgit.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

- **`settings=profile`:** it samples allocations and short lock waits more finely than `default`.
- **`filename`:** use an absolute path that Jeffrey can open. If Jeffrey runs in a container, write into a mounted directory.
- **`dumponexit=true`:** the file is written when the JVM stops, so shut the service down cleanly.
- **`-Dgit.commit`:** it stamps the recording with its commit. Also note whether `git status --porcelain` prints anything, because a build with uncommitted changes isn't the commit it names.

- **Maven:** `-DargLine=`

replays.prompt: My JFR recording counts exceptions, but Jeffrey cannot tell me which types were thrown. How should I record the next one?

runs.reply:
Enable `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow` and turn its throttle off. Add this to your JFR options:

```
-XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,filename=/absolute/path/run.jfr,dumponexit=true,jdk.JavaExceptionThrow#enabled=true,jdk.JavaExceptionThrow#throttle=off
```

**Why your recording only had counts**
- **JDK 21:** `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow` is off in both `default` and `profile`. The recording keeps a count of throwables but can't name them.
- **JDK 25:** the event is on but throttled. It's 300/s under `profile` and 100/s under `default`. The throws it names are then only a sample.
- **JDK 17 or later:** `enabled=true` plus `throttle=off` records every throw. A JDK with no throttle setting, such as 21, warns that `throttle` doesn't exist and ignores it. That's harmless.
- To see which applies to your JDK, check `lib/jfr/profile.jfc` in that JDK.

- Use an absolute path for `filename`, and make sure Jeffrey can read that path. If Jeffrey runs in a container, write into a mounted directory.
- Pass the flag through whatever starts the JVM. That's `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` for a script, Gradle's `jvmArgs`, Maven's `-DargLine=`, or JMH's `-jvmArgsAppend`.
- Record about a minute of steady state, so the exception mix is representative.
- Add `-Dgit.commit=$(git rev-parse HEAD)` so the recording names the commit it came from.
- With throttling off, a throw storm makes the recording noticeably bigger and adds overhead. Keep it for investigation runs.

**Reading it afterwards**
1. Import it with `recordings_analyzeFile(path=..., force=true)`.
2. Check `profiles_summary` to confirm `jdk.JavaExceptionThrow` events are present.
3. Run the `microscope:analyze-exceptions` skill. It separates your application's throws from JVM class-loading noise and traces each type to the code that threw it.

Tell me if you meant a different baseline. `compare_movements` reports no comparability problems for the pair.

## 1. Extra `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM person` before the lookup

**Symptom.** The dom run issues far more COUNT statements than the direct run.

**Evidence.**
- `jdbc_overview` on both profiles: `count_query` runs 11,141 times in dom against 7,163 in direct, which is 3,978 more.
- `code_callSites eventType=jeffrey.JdbcQuery groupBy=name` on dom splits the 11,141 by caller (`PersonRepository#count:151`):

| Caller | Count | Total time | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PersonController#personCount:89` | 7,161 | 2,724.6 ms | 0.38 ms |
| `InefficientPersonService#getRandomPerson` (lambda, line 38) | 3,316 | 1,215.5 ms | 0.37 ms |
| `InefficientPersonService#getNPersons` (lambda, line 52) | 664 | 483.5 ms | 0.73 ms |

**Interpretation.**
- The 7,161 `personCount` calls match direct's 7,163 total, so I take them as the existing baseline traffic. I did not read direct's call sites, so this is an inference.
- The extra ~3,980 COUNTs come from `getRandomPerson` and `getNPersons`. Each of those requests issues exactly one (`perTraceMax` = 1), so this is not an N+1.
- Your 1.2 s matches only the `getRandomPerson` site (1,215.5 ms). Adding the `getNPersons` site makes it **1,699 ms** of COUNT time in total.
- That time is summed over request threads, so it is not a share of the 76 s wall clock.
- I did not check that the `getRandomPerson` and `getNPersons` endpoints are what you call "GET /persons". The profile only names the service methods.

**Recommendation.** Drop or cache the COUNT at `PersonRepository#count` (line 151) on these two paths. I have not opened the source, so this names a frame, not a fix. Verify by re-profiling and checking that `count_query` falls back to about 7,160.

**Confidence.** Medium to high. The counts are direct measurements, but the baseline split is inferred.

## 2. About a quarter more allocation

**Symptom.** The dom run allocates more.

**Evidence.**
- `memory_allocations` / `compare_list` on `jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB`: 4,099,353,541 B in dom against 3,240,636,988 B in direct, which is **+26.5%** over equal-length runs.
- `compare_movements useWeight=true` ranks the movers by self weight:

| Type | Change | Example path (largest single contributor) |
|---|---|---|
| `byte[]` | +379 MiB | `Matcher#appendReplacement` |
| `ArrayList$Itr` | +188.5 MiB | `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedObject#getValue` |
| `String` | +87 MiB | `String#split` |
| `char[]` | +65 MiB | `jdk.jfr.internal.tool.StructuredWriter#flush` |
| Jackson `ObjectNode` → `LinkedHashMap$Entry` | **+8 MiB** | `ObjectNode#put` |

- The candidate-rename pairs show the service methods themselves are close: `getNPersons` 184 MiB (Inefficient) against 178.5 MiB (Efficient), and `getRandomPerson` 61 against 54.5 MiB.

**Interpretation.**
- The +26.5% is real.
- The profile does not support attributing it to JSON tree building. The Jackson node type grew by roughly 8 MiB out of about 820 MiB of net growth.
- Most of the biggest movers have example paths inside `jdk.jfr.*`, which is JFR's own parsing and printing machinery, not the service. Those are the biggest single paths, not the whole story, so I can't rule out other contributions.
- The tree-building claim stays a hypothesis until someone looks at the allocation flamegraph under the controller.

**Recommendation.** None yet. To test it, run `flamegraph_export eventType=jdk.ObjectAllocationInNewTLAB useWeight=true` scoped to `PersonController`. Then re-record both runs with the JFR event-stream consumer excluded.

**Confidence.** High for the +26.5% figure. Low for the cause. This is a single pair of recordings with no variance estimate, and allocation is sampled.
